   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`.    - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]).    - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Serious concern (missing administrative data / complete-case exclusions): Although the June 30, 2023 cutoff provided at least 120 days of post-NOV follow-up, 83 of 1,021 classified failed OWTS records (8.1%) were dropped from the logistic regression models (n = 938) via complete-case deletion due to missing covariate data, alongside 46 unclassified voluntary inspection failures (4.3%) and an unspecified share of 481 initially rejected database records with incomplete/ambiguous reports, with no missingness comparison or sensitivity analysis.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious concern: The study relies on observational logistic regression without quasi-experimental identification and omits major socioeconomic and transactional confounders (household income, wealth/savings, property value, real-estate sale liquidity/escrow arrangements, and baseline failure severity), as explicitly acknowledged on p. 76 (PDF p. 93). Furthermore, three of the four adjusted covariates (new system type used for correction, repair vs. replacement, and correction cost) are post-inspection remediation variables affected by the POS context rather than true baseline confounders.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-weak: The dissertation cites the governing Ohio statutory and administrative rules (ORC Chapter 3718 / 3718.02 and OAC Chapter 3701-29) and PCHD's two-stage 60-day plus 60-day (120-day) Board of Health NOV enforcement procedure, but contains a direct internal contradiction on Portage County's own legal rule—stating on p. 24 (PDF p. 41) that PCHD has NOT adopted a mandatory POS program (offering a voluntary option and not stopping property sales upon failure), yet asserting on p. 84 (PDF p. 101) that Portage County regulations MANDATE POS inspection and repair/replacement prior to property transfer. It also pools four legally distinct non-POS inspection regimes (annual Class I ATU/NPDES, 12-month newly installed OWTS, nuisance complaint, and MS4 stormwater IDDE) into one binary reference group.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Exposure (POS vs. non-POS inspection) and outcome (compliance within 120 days of BOH NOV) were extracted from routine PCHD administrative databases (HDIS, GIS, digital/scanned files), avoiding recall bias, but 46 failed 'voluntary inspections' could not be classified as POS or non-POS, PCHD environmental health staff (the author's own agency) were unblinded to inspection context when signing off compliance, and exact endpoint operationalization (installation date vs. final inspection vs. document completion) has minor definitional ambiguity.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate (adequate for administrative compliance, limited for physical sanitation quality): The outcome captures binary administrative compliance (faulty OWTS correction within <=120 days vs. >120 days after BOH NOV) from local health district enforcement records rather than physical effluent or water-quality measurements, collapses continuous compliance duration into a single 120-day dichotomy, and does not distinguish delayed corrections (>120 days) from permanently uncorrected systems.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan exists. The author reports data-driven model refinement after cleaning ('verifying variable coding, collapsing sparse categories, removing predictors with insufficient data variation', pp. 47-48 / PDF pp. 64-65) and reports regression models only for the dichotomized 120-day 'effective compliance' cutoff despite also defining a 60-day 'restrictive compliance' window and framing the dissertation title around 'compliance duration' without presenting 60-day or continuous survival/time-to-event estimates.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Serious concern: From 1,751 extracted PCHD inspection records (Jan 2, 2015 – June 30, 2023), 481 (27.5%) were excluded during initial cleanup (duplicates, missing PINs/addresses, incomplete/ambiguous reports, or out-of-window dates), 46 failed voluntary inspections were excluded due to indeterminable POS/non-POS status, and 83 of 1,021 failed OWTS cases (8.1%) were excluded from multivariable regression (n = 938) because they lacked complete data on post-inspection remediation covariates (new system type, repair vs. replacement, correction cost, or system age), likely excluding uncorrected non-compliant systems and conditioning inclusion on post-exposure remediation progress.

domain_ratings.justification: Serious risk of bias. First, properties undergoing real estate transfer (POS) differ systematically from properties inspected via nuisance complaints, stormwater IDDE, or annual aeration checks (non-POS) on unmeasured socioeconomic and transactional confounders—including household income, liquid wealth/home-sale proceeds, property value, lender/escrow compulsion, and baseline failure severity—which the author explicitly notes were omitted from the models (Ch. 5, p. 76 / PDF p. 93). Second, three of the four covariates controlled in the adjusted logistic regression (new OWTS type used for correction, repair vs. replacement, and correction cost per $1,000) are post-inspection remediation variables occurring after exposure and directly shaped by POS policy rules (e.g., PCHD prohibits incremental repairs in POS cases while allowing them for owner-occupied non-POS cases; Ch. 5, p. 78 / PDF p. 95), introducing inappropriate post-intervention adjustment.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: Serious risk of bias. Although follow-up appropriately begins at OWTS inspection failure / issuance of the BOH NOV, selection into the regression cohort (n = 938 out of 1,021 classified failed OWTSs) required non-missing values on post-inspection remediation variables ('new system type, correction method, correction cost, and the age of the failing OWTS'; Ch. 3, p. 44 / PDF p. 61; Ch. 4, p. 57 / PDF p. 74). Because new system type, repair/replacement method, and correction expenditure are defined when a remediation plan/installation occurs, excluding the 83 cases lacking these variables conditions participant inclusion on post-intervention remediation progress closely linked to compliance. In addition, 481 of 1,751 initial database records (27.5%) and 46 'voluntary' failed inspections were excluded prior to analysis without disaggregated exclusion counts.

domain_ratings.justification: Moderate risk of bias. Inspection context (POS vs. non-POS) was recorded prospectively at the time of inspection in PCHD's administrative databases (HDIS and permit files), preventing retrospective recall bias. However, 46 failed OWTS inspections ('voluntary inspections', 4.3% of 1,067 failed systems) could not be classified as POS or non-POS and were excluded (Ch. 3, p. 42 / PDF p. 59)—a notable ambiguity given Chapter 2's statement (p. 24 / PDF p. 41) that PCHD's POS program itself is voluntary (which Chapter 5, p. 84 / PDF p. 101 later contradicts by describing Portage County POS inspection and repair before transfer as mandatory). Furthermore, the non-POS comparator pools four heterogeneous inspection mechanisms (annual Class I/NPDES aeration, 12-month new installations, citizen nuisance complaints, and stormwater IDDE) with very different failure profiles.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: Moderate risk of bias. While the author states in Chapters 1-3 that PCHD enforces BOH NOV timelines uniformly across all failed OWTSs (60-day initial NOV plus an automatic 60-day extension to 120 days before legal referral), Chapter 5 reveals an asymmetric regulatory co-intervention: under OAC 3701-29, PCHD allows owner-occupied non-POS households to undertake gradual/incremental repairs while deferring full replacement or sewer connection, whereas POS inspections disallow incremental repairs and require immediate full correction for the pending transfer (Ch. 5, p. 78 / PDF p. 95). Private market co-interventions (escrow holdbacks, lender conditions) also accompany POS cases as part of the real-estate transfer context.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Study S331 (Sarfo 2025) is a retrospective non-randomized comparative administrative study using Portage County Health District (PCHD, Ohio) enforcement records from January 2, 2015, to June 30, 2023 (n = 1,021 failed systems in descriptive tables; n = 938 in multivariable logistic regression) to evaluate whether Point-of-Sale (POS) real-estate transfer OWTS inspections increase timely compliance (<=120 days) with Board of Health Notices of Violation (BOH NOVs) compared with non-POS O&M inspections (annual Class I/NPDES aeration, 12-month new-system, nuisance complaint, and stormwater IDDE inspections). Appraised under ROBINS-I, overall risk of bias is Serious, driven by three Serious-risk domains (D1 Confounding, D2 Selection of participants, and D5 Missing data) and four Moderate-risk domains (D3, D4, D6, D7). Specifically: (1) the observational logistic regressions omit key socioeconomic and real-estate transaction confounders (household income, wealth, property value, sale liquidity, and baseline failure severity) while inappropriately adjusting for three post-inspection remediation variables (new system type, repair vs. replacement, and correction cost) that lie downstream of inspection context; (2) complete-case restriction to 938 of 1,021 failed OWTSs with non-missing remediation type/cost data (alongside 46 excluded 'voluntary' failures and 481 initially excluded records) risks conditioning sample selection on post-exposure remediation progress; and (3) the dissertation contains an unresolved legal contradiction regarding its own study site, stating in Chapter 2 (p. 24) that Portage County's POS program is voluntary and does not halt property sales upon failure, yet claiming in Chapter 5 (p. 84) that Portage County regulations mandate pre-transfer POS inspection and repair/replacement, alongside asymmetric rules allowing incremental repairs in non-POS cases but not POS cases (p. 78). While the large unadjusted compliance gap (63.86% POS vs. 19.85% non-POS within 120 days; crude OR = 7.225; adjusted OR = 4.27) reflects real transactional leverage during property sales, causal attribution to the POS inspection rule itself carries serious risk of bias.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Retrospective non-randomized comparative administrative evaluation (cohort of failed onsite wastewater treatment systems followed for 120-day Notice of Violation compliance, analyzed via unadjusted and multivariable logistic regression)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Primary methods, variable definitions, data cleaning exclusions, and regression specifications are in Definitions (pp. xii-xvii; [PDF Pages 12-17 of 153]) and Chapter 3: Research Methodology (pp. 29-50; Table 1, Figures 1-4; [PDF Pages 46-67 of 153]). Descriptive statistics (n = 1,021), complete-case regression results (n = 938), and VIF diagnostics are in Chapter 4: Results (pp. 53-71; Tables 2-5; [PDF Pages 70-88 of 153]). Local legal/enforcement context, differential incremental-repair rules, and acknowledgment of omitted socioeconomic confounders are in Chapter 1 (pp. 5-7; [PDF Pages 22-24 of 153]), Chapter 2 (p. 24; [PDF Page 41 of 153]), and Chapter 5: Discussion (pp. 72-86; [PDF Pages 89-103 of 153]; note text past PDF Page 103 including Appendices A-B was truncated in prompt delivery, though all core empirical chapters were readable in full).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: ROBINS-I is the exact matching instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 because S331 is a non-randomized empirical evaluation of an administrative/regulatory intervention—Point-of-Sale (POS) OWTS inspection—against a genuine active comparator group (non-POS O&M inspections: annual aeration, newly installed 12-month, nuisance complaint, and stormwater IDDE inspections), following failed OWTSs forward from BOH Notice of Violation issuance over a defined 120-day compliance window. Unlike a cross-sectional prevalence study (JBI Analytical Cross Sectional) or a non-intervention etiological exposure study (JBI Cohort), the dissertation explicitly frames POS inspection as a regulatory O&M program tool whose effectiveness on compliance timeliness is being evaluated.
